mcqs.question: A code assigns A=0, B=01, C=10. Why does this break unambiguous decoding, even though each codeword is distinct?
options: It doesn't break anything — all three codewords are different, so decoding is fine
C's code 10 is the problem because it starts with 1
The codewords are different lengths, which is never allowed in any code
0 is a prefix of 01 (A's code is a prefix of B's code), so a decoder reading '01...' can't tell if it just saw A followed by something starting with 1, or B
mcqs.explanation: Distinctness alone doesn't guarantee unambiguous decoding — the actual requirement is the prefix property. Here 'A'=0 is a prefix of 'B'=01, so upon reading the bit '0', a decoder can't yet tell whether it has a complete codeword (A) or the start of another (B) without look-ahead, which breaks streaming, unambiguous decoding. Variable-length codes are fine as long as the prefix property holds; C=10 isn't itself the issue.

mcqs.question: In Huffman coding, why does the most frequent symbol always end up with the shortest code (or tied for shortest)?
options: Because the greedy merge process always combines the two LEAST frequent nodes first, pushing frequent nodes toward the root and giving them shorter root-to-leaf paths
Because the algorithm assigns codes alphabetically
Because Huffman coding requires all codes to be exactly the same length
It's a coincidence in this specific example, not a general property
mcqs.explanation: Huffman's greedy step always merges the two currently-least-frequent nodes, which means high-frequency nodes get merged later (or not at all until near the root), placing them closer to the root and giving them shorter paths (codes). This is a general, provable property of the algorithm, not a coincidence of this specific example or an alphabetical rule, and Huffman codes are explicitly variable-length by design.

mcqs.question: You gzip a folder that already contains several .zip files, expecting to save more space. What's the most likely outcome?
options: Significant additional savings, since gzip always finds new redundancy
The operation will fail with an error
Little to no savings, and the result may even be slightly larger, since compressed data has already removed most exploitable redundancy
It will restore the files to their original uncompressed size
mcqs.explanation: Already-compressed data looks close to random (high entropy) because its redundancy has already been squeezed out, so there's little to no exploitable structure left for a second compression pass — the result is often about the same size, sometimes marginally larger due to format overhead. This is a direct consequence of the source coding theorem's entropy floor, not a tooling limitation.
